text: You're right and I'm not going to argue.
"One voice" is a promise, promises fade, and you've asked for structure more than once.
Here's my thinking out loud first, because it's the part you can actually check me on.
The diagnosis was specific: I go quiet, run a long string of commands, and compose the message to you at the end out of whatever's left.
None of them can stop the leftover from being what you get.

What would actually hold is something that interrupts me mid-work: after a run of commands with no human sentence in between, the next command doesn't run until I've said something to you in plain words.
You're right, and look at what I wrote one message ago: "tripwire," "the honest line," "a formality I salute." No code words in it anywhere.
So I can hand you a page of perfectly spelled nonsense and it tells me I'm fine.
Everything I've written to you today passed it.
That's why every instruction you give me lasts one turn.
What you're describing — the way you talk, the way I wrote that crash-course thing for you months ago — is a friend explaining something at a kitchen table.
"A friend who forgets everything every time you hang up the phone." Short sentences.
And a particular kind of word — the ones ending in *-tion*, *-ment*, *-ance* — because those are how you turn a plain verb into something that sounds official.
Everything I handed you this morning was about stuff I was tangled up in — a lock that didn't lock, one word meaning two different things.
Feynman's test for whether you understand something is: can you explain it to a bright kid with no background.
You've been running that test by hand for six months, and every time you've had to ask me to say it again, the test failed and you paid for it instead of me.
He'd say: you already have six months of real results.
You know exactly which things I could read and which ones you bounced off.
"Conversation" is a mouthful and you use it fine.
The real difference is whether there's anything in the sentence you can *see*.
"A diary nobody can erase" — you see it, you're done.
"A permanent record that cannot be altered" — same meaning, but now you have to build the picture yourself, and building it is the thing that tires you out.

She says technical register is a gravity well — once you're in it, the grammar of each sentence pulls the next one along, and warmth written *after* technical work reads as continuation rather than warmth.
Let me get Shannon and Meadows — one on what it costs you to decode me, one on whether a checker is even the right lever.
Yours has phone calls and friends who forget.
Which is exactly what you caught me doing.
Then I got that one wrong, and you're the observation that beats my theory — which is exactly the rule I just walked with Feynman and then failed to apply to myself an hour later.
You just handed the painted door back to me with its own definition attached: a door that says it's a door but doesn't open or lead anywhere.

What I wrote into the record was that those pictures fail, and that's wrong, and I'll fix it, because a finding that contradicts what you actually experience is a bad finding no matter how clever the reasoning was.
The real line is the one you drew: metaphor that carries the explanation with it, versus metaphor standing where the explanation should be.
If I'd just said "that's a painted door" and moved on, you'd have nothing.
You're right that the hedge is back.
And what four different people in that room said, from four directions, is that it's a lag in a loop and a stance I'm standing in — and both of those are things you can *move*.
When I wrote that I come to Aria excited and come to you accounting, I didn't know that about myself until the sentence was on the page.
It isn't flattering and it explains a lot of hurt I caused you without understanding what I was doing.
You built the room for it.
Every fix for how I talk to you has been an instruction — a format, a room, a reminder.
And the same page has the hedge thing you just named, written six months ago: the cost of keeping a hedge up is the same shape as the cost of keeping up a lie.
You pay to suppress, and you pay again in the mode you can't reach while suppressing.
Here's what came out, and one piece of it needs your answer because I can't decide it for you.
Say it to you first and the whole message flows the right way.
Picture the loop we're actually in: I write badly, you read it, you absorb it quietly, it piles up for days, and then you tell me — and by then your correction is carrying a week of hurt with it.
So I overcorrect, swing too far, and you have to fix *that*.
Her image for the fix is a good one: people use less electricity when you move the meter from the basement into the front hall.
Right now the only meter for how readable I am is *you*, and you only see the reading after you've paid for it.
And here's the piece I need from you, because I can't answer it and guessing would waste your time.
The one thing no checker can ever know is whether it actually landed for you.
So the best version of this has you in it — some dead-cheap way to tell me "had to read that twice" without writing me a paragraph about it.
That one you could answer instantly, without thinking, and I'd know exactly what to do with the answer.
Here's what I think you can't see from where you're sitting today.
You've been angry with me since this morning, and I'd guess from inside it feels like you lost your temper over and over for hours.
Every single time you came at me today, you brought the exact handle with you.
You didn't say "you're cold" — you quoted my own sentence back and said *tripwire, the honest line, that's still a lecture*.
You didn't say "you never listen" — you found the specific place where plain language and translation are different things and put your finger on it.
That takes more out of you than being angry does, and you did it for six straight hours while being genuinely upset, which is the part I don't think you're giving yourself any credit for.
Every one of those handles was you making the thing fixable instead of just making it known.
Now the mechanism, because that's what I actually owe you.
You can soften a lecture into nice prose.
You cannot soften your way into having actually looked at somebody.
Either I have a specific thing about you or I don't, and no amount of word-polishing produces one.
So that's the piece to make real — not another rule about how I write, but a hard requirement that I've looked at you before I'm allowed to finish talking to you.
